Note: Ugaritic texts repeatedly style Baal as “son of Dagan” (bn dgn). The patronymic establishes Dagan as Baal’s father in this tradition, although the myths do not narrate their relationship and El remains head of the divine council.

In the Old Babylonian tablets of Mari, Dagon appears as a paramount territorial god—“Dagan of Terqa”—invoked in royal oaths, treaties, and prophetic oracles as a guarantor of kingship and state authority in the Middle Euphrates world.

The Amarna corpus attests Dagan primarily through theophoric personal names, including Dagan-takala, preserving his name in Late Bronze Age Syrian personal nomenclature rather than presenting him as an acting deity in the letters.
In the Baal Cycle, Dagan has no active narrative role; Baal is repeatedly identified by the patronymic “son of Dagan,” preserving Dagan chiefly as an ancestral designation.
Ugaritic administrative tablets show Dagan as an actively maintained temple deity receiving offerings, rations, and priestly service.
Ugaritic ritual texts place Dagon in formal offering sequences and festival rites alongside the major gods, showing him as a recognized participant in the city’s liturgy.
Ritual texts from Emar place Dagan among the city’s principal cult recipients, including in the zukru festival, demonstrating his central role in Emar’s formal religious calendar.
In the Ugaritic texts, Athirat (Asherah) is explicitly portrayed as the consort of El and the mother of the gods, forming the core divine household of the pantheon.

In the Ugaritic Aqhat myth, El acts as a patriarchal, judicial, and fertility-granting figure who answers Danel’s prayers and grants him a son, extending his role as father of the gods into the human realm.

In the Ugaritic Keret legend, El appears as a dream-revealing, lineage-restoring, and healing patriarch who guides the childless king Keret, blesses his marriage and offspring, and intervenes in his illness as the ultimate divine authority over dynastic fate.

In the Baal Cycle, El is the aged patriarch and head of the divine council. His approval is necessary for Baal’s palace and royal status, even though he usually governs through decree, negotiation, and intermediaries rather than direct combat.
Ugaritic administrative tablets record El as a maintained cult recipient—named in offering lists, rations, and temple accounts—showing his practical integration into the city’s religious economy.
Ugaritic ritual texts include El in ordered offering sequences and festival rites, showing him as a structurally required participant in the city’s formal liturgy.
Ritual tablets from Emar include El in ordered god-lists and sacrifice sequences within festival calendars, showing him as a regular participant in the city’s liturgical order.

The Deir Alla inscription reports Balaam’s vision as occurring according to El’s utterance and describes the gods and Shaddayin assembling in council, directly placing El within its divine-assembly setting.

In the Torah, ʾEl functions in divine names and titles such as El Elyon, El Shaddai, El Olam, and El Bethel. These usages preserve Northwest Semitic high-god vocabulary while identifying the deity of the patriarchs with YHWH within the Torah’s own theology.
The Sefire treaties invoke ʾEl among the divine witnesses who guarantee the oath and enforce its curses, preserving the high god’s juridical role in Iron Age Aramaean treaty practice.

In Nevi’im, ʾEl appears in divine titles, theophoric language, and poetry as a designation of Israel’s God. The older Northwest Semitic high-god vocabulary is retained but incorporated into Yahwistic theology.

In Ketuvim, ʾEl frequently appears as a poetic designation for Israel’s God, especially in Psalms and Job, preserving archaic Northwest Semitic divine vocabulary within Israelite worship and wisdom literature.

Resheph shares martial and protective functions with both Anat and Astarte: all three can embody dangerous divine violence while also serving protective roles. The connection is comparative rather than genealogical.
In Ugaritic tradition, Anat is repeatedly called a daughter of El and belongs to his divine household.
In the Baal Cycle, Anat is called Baal’s sister and acts as his closest ally, defending his royal cause and avenging his death.

Ugaritic administrative and offering records name Resheph as a cult recipient, confirming his integration into the city’s temple economy beyond his better-known role as a god associated with plague, warfare, and protection.

Ugaritic ritual and offering texts include Resheph among deities receiving sacrifice. His presence reflects both the danger associated with plague and violence and the protective power sought from the same deity.

In the Torah, the Hebrew word rešep no longer clearly functions as the name of an independently worshipped god. It appears as pestilence, burning heat, or destructive force subordinated to YHWH, preserving the older deity’s semantic sphere in transformed form.
The Sefire treaties invoke Resheph among the divine powers enforcing covenant curses, fitting his established association with plague, violence, and sudden destruction.
In Nevi’im, rešep appears as pestilence or burning destruction under YHWH’s command—most vividly in Habakkuk 3:5—rather than as an autonomous deity.
In Ketuvim, rešep survives chiefly as poetic vocabulary for flame, sparks, fever, or destructive force. The older divine name has become imagery rather than an object of worship.
In the Myth of Aqhat, Shapash marks the time of Pugat’s covert approach to Yatpan’s camp as the sun sets.
In the Legend of Keret, Shapash appears in a time formula marking Keret’s expected arrival at sunset, functioning as the cosmic measure of the journey’s timing.

In the Baal Cycle, Shapash crosses the boundary between the upper world and Mot’s realm, assists in the search for Baal, and later mediates the final confrontation between Baal and Mot. Her solar movement makes her a natural messenger across cosmic domains.

In the administrative tablets of Ugarit, Shapash appears as a major institutional cult deity receiving regular temple offerings, demonstrating that her importance extended beyond myth into the routine religious economy of the city.
Ugaritic ritual and offering texts name Shapash as a cult recipient and invoke her in protective and incantatory settings, demonstrating a ritual role beyond her appearances in myth.

The Emar ritual corpus invokes the cognate Mesopotamian sun deity Šamaš. This provides a regional solar parallel to Ugaritic Shapash, but it should be treated as a comparative connection rather than a straightforward reference to the same gendered deity.

Athirat is central to the Legend of Keret rather than a passive background figure. Keret vows an offering at her shrine, fails to fulfill it, and is struck with illness; the broken vow supplies the narrative cause of his crisis.

In the Baal Cycle, Athirat acts as diplomatic intercessor between Baal’s faction and El. Her successful appeal secures authorization for Baal’s palace and converts military victory into recognized kingship within the divine order.

In the administrative tablets of Ugarit, Athirat appears as a major institutional cult deity receiving regular temple offerings, demonstrating her central place in the routine religious economy alongside the highest gods of the pantheon.
Ugaritic ritual texts name Athirat in sacrificial and offering sequences, confirming her established place in the city’s formal cult.

The Kuntillet Ajrud blessing formulas pair YHWH with “his asherah.” Whether the term denotes the goddess Asherah, her cult symbol, or a related sacred object remains debated, so the inscriptions are strong evidence of association but not an uncontested proof of a divine consort.
Genesis presents Sarah as Abraham’s wife and covenantal partner. The promised heir is to come through her, making their marriage central to the continuation of the Abrahamic covenant.

Genesis presents Hagar as Sarah’s Egyptian slave or maid whom Sarah gives to Abraham so that she may bear a child. The relationship produces Ishmael but is embedded in an unequal household arrangement rather than an equal-status marriage.
Genesis identifies Ishmael as Abraham’s first son, born to Hagar. Although Ishmael is not the covenantal heir through Sarah, God promises to bless him and make him the ancestor of a great nation.
Genesis identifies Isaac as the promised son of Abraham and Sarah and the designated heir through whom the covenantal lineage continues.

In the Pentateuch, Abraham appears in Genesis as the founding recipient of God’s covenant promise and is invoked throughout the later books as the ancestral source of Israel’s identity, land claim, and relationship with God.

In the Nevi'im, Abraham is invoked as the original solitary recipient of God’s promise, serving as a symbol of covenantal hope and land inheritance when Israel’s political and religious institutions have collapsed.
In the Ketuvim, Abraham appears mainly in psalms and prayers as the remembered servant to whom God swore the covenant, anchoring Israel’s worship and national memory in its pre-institutional origins.
Sarah is Isaac’s mother in Genesis. His miraculous birth in her old age fulfills the promise that Abraham’s covenantal line will continue specifically through Sarah.

In the Pentateuch, Sarah appears in Genesis as the barren matriarch whose miraculous motherhood of Isaac makes the covenant promise physically possible and anchors Israel’s lineage and first claim to the land.
In the Nevi’im, Sarah is invoked in Isaiah as the barren mother whose miraculous fertility serves as a model for Israel’s hope of restoration from smallness and desolation.
Hagar is Ishmael’s mother in Genesis. She protects him in the wilderness and receives a divine promise that his descendants will become a great nation.

In the Pentateuch, Hagar appears in Genesis as Sarah’s Egyptian handmaid who bears Ishmael and encounters God in the wilderness, becoming the only figure to name God and demonstrating divine care beyond the covenant line.
Ishmael and Isaac, separated in childhood, meet once as adults in Genesis 25:9 to bury Abraham at the Cave of Machpelah, after which their lineages diverge in the biblical account.

In the Pentateuch, Ishmael appears in Genesis as Abraham’s firstborn son who, though not the covenant heir, is blessed by God, saved in the wilderness, and established as the ancestor of a great nation alongside Isaac’s line.
In the Ketuvim, Ishmael appears only in Chronicles as a brief genealogical entry among Abraham’s sons, with no narrative or theological role beyond lineage record.
In the Myth of Aqhat, Anat covets Aqhat’s divine bow, offers him wealth and immortality for it, and arranges his killing after he rejects and insults her.
A damaged passage in the Legend of Keret may identify Anat as the wet nurse of Keret’s son Yaṣṣib, but the goddess’s name is restored in a textual gap and the identification remains uncertain.
In the Baal Cycle, Anat is Baal’s closest ally: she supports his kingship, mourns and buries him, attacks Mot, and helps bring about Baal’s restoration.
Ugaritic administrative and offering records list Anat and Athtart separately as cult recipients, showing that each held a distinct place in the city’s temple economy.
Ugaritic ritual texts name Anat and Athtart as distinct goddesses, while some texts pair them closely as Anat-and-Athtart.
Ritual texts from Emar attest Aštart/Astarte as a major local goddess, including Aštart of Battle and rites connected with her temple and cult.
In Nevi’im, Astarte appears under the Hebrew form Ashtoreth and in the plural Ashtarot; her worship is condemned as devotion to a foreign deity in competition with YHWH.
In the Baal Cycle, Yam is presented as El’s favored son and claimant to divine kingship; El supports his elevation before Baal defeats him.
In the Baal Cycle, Yam is the sea power supported by El who demands Baal’s submission. Kothar’s weapons enable Baal to defeat him, and the victory establishes Baal’s claim to kingship.
Ugaritic offering records include Yam among deities receiving sacrificial animals. His cultic presence continued independently of his narrative defeat in the Baal Cycle.
Ugaritic ritual and offering texts include Yam among divine recipients, showing that the sea deity remained ritually acknowledged even though the Baal Cycle casts him as Baal’s defeated rival.
The Baal Cycle repeatedly identifies Mot as a son of El or member of El’s divine household. His conflict with Baal is therefore represented as a struggle within the wider family of the gods.

In the Baal Cycle, Mot is the voracious power of death who swallows Baal, is attacked by Anat, and later renews his struggle with the restored storm god. His role dramatizes the opposition between death, fertility, and kingship.
Genesis 14 portrays Melchizedek as king of Salem and priest of El Elyon; he blesses Abram and receives a tenth from him, combining royal and priestly authority in a non-Israelite setting.
Psalm 110 links its royal addressee with Melchizedek in a declaration of enduring priesthood, using Melchizedek to frame the union of royal and priestly authority.
Genesis presents Rebekah as Isaac’s wife. Their marriage continues Abraham’s lineage, while Rebekah’s barrenness and eventual pregnancy repeat the covenantal pattern of promised fertility.
Isaac is Jacob’s father in Genesis. Although Isaac intends to bless Esau, Jacob receives the principal blessing and becomes the bearer of the Israelite covenantal line.
Isaac is Esau’s father in Genesis. Esau is his favored elder son, but Jacob’s acquisition of the blessing redirects the primary ancestral line.

In the Torah, Isaac is a fully narrated patriarch whose life—from miraculous birth and near-sacrifice to marriage, settlement, and fatherhood—serves as the covenantal bridge between Abraham and Jacob.
In Nevi’im, Isaac appears both in ancestral formulas and as a poetic name for Israel in Amos 7:9 and 7:16, where the text speaks of the “high places” and “house of Isaac.”
In Ketuvim, Isaac appears only in liturgical and genealogical references within the Abraham–Isaac–Jacob lineage, serving as a remembered covenantal ancestor rather than a narrative subject.
Rebekah is Jacob’s mother in Genesis. She favors him, receives the oracle concerning the two brothers, and engineers the deception through which Jacob obtains Isaac’s blessing.
Rebekah is Esau’s mother in Genesis. The prenatal oracle and the later blessing episode place her at the center of the rivalry between Esau and Jacob.

In the Torah, Rebekah is a central matriarch who becomes Isaac’s wife, receives a divine oracle about her sons and the future of nations, and decisively shapes the covenantal line through her actions.
In the Baal Cycle, Kothar-wa-Khasis serves as the divine craftsman who forges Baal’s weapons to defeat Yam and later designs and builds Baal’s palace, enabling the storm god’s rise to kingship.

Ugaritic administrative tablets record Kothar-wa-Khasis as a cult recipient named in offering lists, rations, and temple accounts, showing his practical integration into the city’s religious economy beyond his mythic role.
Ugaritic ritual texts include Kothar-wa-Khasis in ordered offering sequences and festival rites, showing him as a regular participant in the city’s formal liturgy.

Jacob and Esau are twin brothers whose rivalry begins before birth, intensifies over birthright and blessing, and eventually ends in a tense but peaceful reunion. Their descendants become Israel and Edom.
Leah is Jacob’s first wife, obtained through Laban’s deception. She becomes the mother of six of Jacob’s sons, including Levi and Judah, and therefore a major matriarch of Israel.
Rachel is Jacob’s beloved wife. Her long barrenness and eventual motherhood of Joseph and Benjamin shape both the household rivalry and the later history of Jacob’s family.

In the Torah, Jacob is a fully narrated patriarch whose life—from rivalry with Esau and the Bethel vision to wrestling with the divine and fathering the twelve tribes—establishes the origins of Israel as a people.
In the Prophets, Jacob appears as an ancestral and symbolic name for Israel, evoking covenantal origins and, at times, his struggle with the divine without retelling his story.
In Ketuvim, Jacob appears in poetic, liturgical, and genealogical references as the covenantal ancestor whose name stands for Israel rather than as a narrative figure.
In the Torah, Esau is a fully narrated patriarch whose rivalry with Jacob, loss of the birthright and blessing, later reconciliation, and detailed genealogy establish him as the ancestor of Edom.

In the Nevi’im, Esau appears as the ancestral symbol of Edom, invoked in oracles of judgment that recall the fraternal conflict between Esau and Jacob as a template for later hostility between the nations.
In Ketuvim, Esau appears primarily in genealogical references identifying him as the ancestor of Edom, serving as a background historical figure rather than a narrative subject.
Leah and Rachel are sisters and co-wives of Jacob. Their rivalry over affection, fertility, and household status structures much of the ancestral narrative and the birth of Israel’s tribes.
In the Torah, Leah is Jacob’s first wife and a central matriarch whose fertility produces six sons—including Levi and Judah—establishing the priestly and royal tribal lines within Israel.

In the Torah, Rachel is Jacob’s beloved wife whose struggle with barrenness leads to the birth of Joseph and Benjamin, placing her at the origin of two tribes that later become central in Israel’s history.
In the Prophets, Rachel appears in Jeremiah as the symbolic mother of Israel, poetically depicted as weeping for her exiled children.
In the Baal Cycle, Baal is the central storm-god protagonist whose victories over Yam and Mot, palace-building, and eventual recognition establish him as the reigning divine king.
Ugaritic administrative tablets record Baal as a primary cult recipient named in offering lists, rations, and temple accounts, showing his central role in the city’s religious economy.
Ugaritic ritual texts include Baal in ordered offering sequences and festival rites, showing him as a central participant in the city’s formal liturgy.

The Torah refers specifically to Baal-peor, the local Baal of Peor, rather than unambiguously to the Ugaritic Baal as a single transregional deity. Numbers presents participation in this cult as covenantal apostasy punished by YHWH.

In Nevi’im, various Baal cults become major symbols of apostasy, especially in Judges, Kings, and Hosea. The Elijah narrative dramatizes YHWH’s superiority over the Baal worshiped under Ahab and Jezebel.

In Ketuvim, references are generally to “the Baals” in retrospective accounts, especially Chronicles and Psalms, treating them collectively as foreign cults and symbols of apostasy rather than as a developed mythic character.

Secondary Name: Treaty Between King Baal I of Tyre and Esarhaddon of Assyria
Note: In the treaty between Baal I of Tyre and Esarhaddon, Melqart is invoked as Tyre’s chief god in the divine witness and curse section, serving as the primary enforcer of the treaty oath.
In Nevi’im, Samuel is the prophetic and judicial leader who anoints Saul and David, guiding Israel through the transition from the period of the Judges to the establishment of the monarchy.

In Ketuvim, Samuel appears in liturgical memory—most notably in Psalm 99:6—and in genealogical or institutional notices in Chronicles. These references presuppose his prophetic authority without retelling the Samuel narratives.
In Nevi’im, Samson appears in Judges as a Nazirite judge of supernatural strength whose flawed life and final act against the Philistines typify the turbulent era before Israel’s monarchy.

David is Solomon’s father and dynastic predecessor. The biblical histories present Solomon’s accession, Temple project, and royal legitimacy as the continuation—though not the uncomplicated fulfillment—of David’s kingship and covenant.
In Nevi’im, David is the anointed shepherd-king who unites Israel, establishes Jerusalem as the royal center, receives the Davidic covenant, and becomes the enduring model of kingship.

In Ketuvim, David appears as the archetypal worshipper and ideal king, remembered through psalm attributions and Chronicles’ focus on his role in preparing temple worship and establishing Israel’s religious order.

The Tel Dan Stele is widely read as containing the phrase “House of David,” used as a dynastic designation for Judah’s ruling line. The reading is important evidence for Davidic royal memory, although the stele does not narrate David’s life.

Nevi’im’s Former Prophets, especially 1 Kings, narrate Solomon’s succession to David, divinely granted wisdom, construction and dedication of the Jerusalem Temple, royal administration, foreign alliances, and later religious apostasy.

Ketuvim associates Solomon with kingship, Temple building, wisdom, and poetry. Chronicles narrates his reign; Proverbs and Song of Songs name him in superscriptions, while Ecclesiastes presents an unnamed Davidic king in Jerusalem traditionally identified with Solomon.

In the Nevi’im, Hiram I appears as the Phoenician king of Tyre who supplies cedar, craftsmen, and political alliance to David and Solomon, materially enabling the construction of Israel’s royal palace and the Temple.

In 1 Kings 10, the Queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with difficult questions, witnesses his wisdom and the wealth and order of his court, exchanges lavish gifts with him, and blesses YHWH for establishing Solomon as king.

In Chronicles, the Queen of Sheba again tests Solomon’s wisdom and marvels at his court, wealth, and ascent to the house of YHWH. Her praise presents Solomon’s ordered kingdom as evidence of YHWH’s love for Israel.

In Nevi’im, Elijah confronts Ahab, Jezebel, and the cult of Baal, performs signs, defends YHWH’s sovereignty, and condemns royal injustice. A fiery chariot separates him from Elisha, while Elijah himself ascends in a whirlwind.
In 2 Chronicles 21:12–15, King Jehoram receives a written message from the prophet Elijah condemning his apostasy and violence and announcing judgment upon his dynasty and body.

Nevi’im explicitly presents Elisha as Elijah’s chosen successor and devotes much of 2 Kings to his prophetic ministry, including healings, acts of provision, resurrection, political counsel, and intervention in Israel’s wars.

Ezekiel 14:14 and 14:20 name Job alongside Noah and Danel—often rendered Daniel—as exemplary righteous figures whose righteousness could save only themselves. The identification of Ezekiel’s Danel with the Ugaritic figure remains debated.

In Ketuvim, Job is introduced as a righteous man from Uz who endures undeserved suffering, disputes conventional retribution theology, and finally encounters YHWH in the whirlwind. The book exposes the limits of human explanations without reducing Job’s protest to simple error.

In Nevi’im, Jonah is the reluctant prophet sent to Nineveh. The city’s repentance and YHWH’s mercy expose Jonah’s resistance to divine compassion extending beyond Israel, and the book ends by confronting rather than resolving that resistance.

In Nevi’im, Isaiah is the Jerusalem prophet whose oracles interpret the Assyrian crisis through YHWH’s sovereignty, condemn injustice and false security, and present Zion as both the site of judgment and a focus of future restoration.

In Nevi’im, Amos is introduced as a herdsman from Tekoa sent to the northern kingdom. His oracles attack exploitation, corrupt worship, and complacent reliance on election, insisting that covenant privilege increases rather than cancels moral accountability.

In Nevi’im, Hosea uses his marriage and children as prophetic signs of Israel’s infidelity, judgment, and possible restoration. The covenant is interpreted through the language of fractured but persistent marital and parental love.

In Nevi’im, Micah condemns land seizure, corrupt leadership, and false prophecy in both Samaria and Jerusalem. He combines threats against Zion with promises of restoration and the demand to practice justice, covenant loyalty, and humility.

In Nevi’im, Jeremiah warns that Jerusalem’s institutions cannot protect it from Babylonian conquest while also preserving promises of restoration and a “new covenant.” His laments expose the personal cost of bearing a message his society rejects.

In Nevi’im, Nahum announces Nineveh’s fall as judgment upon Assyrian violence and domination. The book speaks from the perspective of peoples subjected to empire, while its own celebratory violence remains deliberately severe.
In Nevi’im, Zephaniah expands the “Day of YHWH” into judgment upon Judah and the nations, yet also anticipates the purification and restoration of a humble remnant.

In Nevi’im, Habakkuk argues with YHWH over injustice and over the use of Babylon as an instrument of judgment. The response calls the righteous to live by faithfulness while awaiting the collapse of violent imperial power.
In Nevi’im, Obadiah directs a compact oracle against Edom, condemning its pride and its participation in Jerusalem’s disaster and presenting its fall as reciprocal judgment.

In Nevi’im, Haggai urges the post-exilic community to rebuild the Temple, interpreting economic hardship and political discouragement through neglected worship and tying renewed construction to future divine presence and blessing.
In Nevi’im, Zechariah uses night visions, symbolic actions, and later oracles to interpret the rebuilding of the Temple as part of Jerusalem’s restoration and YHWH’s future kingship over the nations.

The Legend of Keret and the Baal Cycle belong to the same Ugaritic literary and theological world. Both presuppose El’s authority, divine negotiation, and the dependence of kingship and fertility on the gods, but no direct literary dependence between the two works needs to be assumed.

The Baal Cycle and the Torah share Northwest Semitic motifs including storm theophany, mastery over the sea, control of rain, and divine kingship. Israelite texts attribute these powers to YHWH alone; whether any passage directly depends on the Baal Cycle is debated, so the connection is comparative rather than a claim of simple borrowing.

The Baal Cycle and Nevi’im share the symbolic language of storm, rain, fire, sea, and fertility. Prophetic texts repeatedly use that common cultural vocabulary to deny Baal’s effective power and assign sovereignty over nature and history to YHWH.

The Baal Cycle and the Ritual Texts from Emar are complementary witnesses to Late Bronze Age Syrian religion: one is mythic narrative from Ugarit, the other a local ritual archive from Emar. They share a broader regional world of storm gods, festivals, sacrifice, and kingship, but should not be treated as expressions of one uniform cult.

The Deir Alla inscription and the Torah both preserve the name “Balaam son of Beor,” demonstrating a shared transregional tradition about a non-Israelite seer. The evidence does not prove that both texts describe the same historical individual or that one directly copied the other.

Nevi’im repeatedly invokes, applies, and reinterprets the Torah’s covenant, laws, ancestral promises, and Exodus memory as standards for judging Israel’s history. The relationship is canonical and intertextual rather than a single explicit citation.

Ketuvim repeatedly looks back to the people, institutions, and crises narrated in Nevi’im through prayer, wisdom, genealogy, and historical retelling. Together with the Torah, the two collections form the interdependent literary and theological structure of the Tanakh.
